ambiguities.impact: The natural contract uses a nonnegative perturbation radius, but that sign condition must be made explicit in a formal statement.
ambiguities.issue: The lemma does not separately quantify epsilon or print epsilon >= 0. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Lemma 2.2, perturbation inequality.)

ambiguities.evidence: The proof uses sign(ell_j(x)), which directly describes the real case; no complex phase convention is supplied. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: proof of Lemma 2.2.)
ambiguities.impact: The inequality itself extends through absolute-value estimates, but the paper's displayed attainment argument should not be copied unchanged into a complex formalization.
ambiguities.issue: The paper does not explicitly declare whether the scalar data are real or complex. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Section 2 and proof of Lemma 2.2.)

contract_plain_english: Any componentwise relative perturbation of the n+1 data values by at most epsilon changes the exact interpolated value at fixed x by at most epsilon times cond(x,n,f) in relative terms; this is an exact finite inequality and requires the original value to be nonzero. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Definition 2.1 and Lemma 2.2.)

source_evidence.observation: The interpolation points and evaluation point are fixed, the vector f varies, and vector inequalities are componentwise.
The relative condition number is defined for p_f(x) != 0 using componentwise perturbations satisfying |Delta f| <= epsilon |f|.
The lemma states that for any Delta f satisfying the componentwise perturbation condition, the exact relative output change is at most cond(x,n,f) epsilon.
The proof invokes the exact linear dependence of the interpolated value on Delta f and then says the perturbation inequality follows trivially.

statement.algorithm_linkage: The bound compares two exact interpolants, p_f and p_{f+Delta f}; it is not a rounding-error statement about either barycentric evaluation formula. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Definition 2.1 and Lemma 2.2.)
binders: An interpolation parameter n, distinct nodes x_j, data f_j for j=0,...,n, and a fixed evaluation point x are in scope. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Section 2 opening paragraph.)
The claim quantifies over any data perturbation Delta f satisfying |Delta f| <= epsilon |f| componentwise. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Lemma 2.2, perturbation inequality.)
conclusions: For every admissible Delta f, |p_f(x)-p_{f+Delta f}(x)|/|p_f(x)| <= cond(x,n,f) epsilon. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Lemma 2.2, perturbation inequality.)
constants_and_indexing: The perturbation factor is exactly epsilon cond(x,n,f), with no additional numerical constant. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Lemma 2.2, perturbation inequality.)
The underlying interpolation and condition-number sums contain the n+1 indices j=0,...,n. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: equations (2.1) and (2.2).)
definitions_and_conventions: p_f(x)=sum_{j=0}^n f_j ell_j(x), with ell_j the Lagrange basis from equation (2.1). (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: equation (2.1).)

cond(x,n,f)=lim_{eta->0} sup { |p_f(x)-p_{f+Delta f}(x)|/[eta |p_f(x)|] : |Delta f| <= eta |f| }, where eta merely distinguishes the definition's limiting variable from the finite-bound notation. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Definition 2.1.)
Lemma 2.2 evaluates this condition number as sum_{j=0}^n |ell_j(x)f_j|/|p_n(x)|. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: equation (2.2).)
Vector inequalities are componentwise. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Section 2 opening paragraph.)
error_notions: Input error is componentwise relative data error, |Delta f_j| <= epsilon |f_j|. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Lemma 2.2, perturbation hypothesis.)
Output error is relative scalar error at x, |p_f(x)-p_{f+Delta f}(x)|/|p_f(x)|. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Lemma 2.2, perturbation conclusion.)
The multiplier is the condition number evaluated at the original data f, not at f+Delta f. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Lemma 2.2, perturbation inequality.)
exceptional_values: The relative bound excludes p_f(x)=0 through the condition-number definition. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Definition 2.1.)
If f_j=0, the componentwise hypothesis forces Delta f_j=0; this follows directly from |Delta f_j| <= epsilon |f_j|. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Definition 2.1 and Lemma 2.2.)
higher_order_terms: The finite perturbation inequality has no O(epsilon^2) or other omitted term. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Lemma 2.2, perturbation inequality.)
hypotheses: p_n is the degree-at-most-n polynomial interpolating f_j at the distinct points x_j. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Section 2 opening paragraph.)
The nodes x_j and evaluation point x are held fixed while f is perturbed. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Section 2 opening paragraph.)
The exact value p_f(x)=p_n(x) is nonzero. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Definition 2.1.)
The admissible perturbation obeys |Delta f_j| <= epsilon |f_j| for every j. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Definition 2.1 and Lemma 2.2.)
implicit_context: The displayed inequality is a finite, exact consequence of linear interpolation in f, even though cond itself was introduced through an infinitesimal limit. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Definition 2.1, Lemma 2.2, and its proof.)
The perturbation changes only the function data; it does not perturb x or any x_j. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Section 2 opening paragraph.)
norms: The paper uses scalar absolute values and componentwise vector comparison, with no vector norm. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Section 2 opening paragraph and Lemma 2.2.)
numerical_model: There is no floating-point precision or rounding model in this claim; Delta f is an abstract exact data perturbation. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Definition 2.1 and Lemma 2.2.)

undebatable_constraints: The quantifier is over every Delta f satisfying the componentwise bound. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Lemma 2.2.)
The compared quantities are the exact values p_f(x) and p_{f+Delta f}(x). (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Lemma 2.2.)
The output denominator is |p_f(x)|, so p_f(x) must be nonzero. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Definition 2.1 and Lemma 2.2.)
The right-hand side is cond(x,n,f) epsilon without a remainder term. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Lemma 2.2.)
Perturbations of nodes or of the evaluation point are outside this claim. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 548, anchor: Section 2 opening paragraph.)
